transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I... I honestly didn't know if I should come in, but it's just gotten to the point where I can't function at work anymore. I'm a high school teacher, and, well, part of my job involves recording these lesson videos for the students to review online or for the ones who are out sick. It seemed like a good idea at first, you know, to help them catch up, but... but now it's become this absolute nightmare for me. 

When I watch the playback to check the audio or make sure the whiteboard is in frame, I just... I can’t stop seeing this crooked, completely swollen-looking side of my face. It’s right there on the screen, glaring back at me. It just looks so lopsided and wrong. And it’s not just a passing thought, it’s like, once I notice it—which is immediately, every single time—I can't see anything else. I'll sit there pausing and rewinding the video just staring at how bad it is. 

And the worst part is, it bleeds into the rest of my day. When I'm actually standing up there in front of the classroom, I can't even focus on teaching because I feel like the students must just be staring at my face. I mean, how could they not? It's so obvious. And it's not just the kids, it's the parents when they watch the videos at home, or the other staff members in the hallways and the breakroom... I'm trying to explain the curriculum or talk about a student's progress, and in my head, I just know they aren't listening to a single word I'm saying. They're just fixated on how swollen and crooked my face is. It's exhausting, it really is, just constantly knowing everyone is staring at it all day long...
Is it always this particular part of your face that bothers you, or are there other parts of your body that you also worry about?

No, it's... I mean, it's just my face. That's the only thing. But honestly, that's more than enough, isn't it? I mean, it's not like I can just put a sweater over it or hide it in a pair of loose pants. It's my face. It's the very first thing anyone sees when they look at me. And it's not just a general feeling of being unattractive, it's this specific, undeniable... asymmetry. The swelling on the one side, the way it throws everything off balance. 

I don't really think about my arms or my stomach or anything like that. I go to the gym sometimes, I try to stay reasonably fit, and I don't obsess over any of that. If my shirt fits a little tight, whatever. But my face... I can't escape it. I've spent hours—literally hours—just standing in front of the bathroom mirror, turning my head slightly to the left, then to the right, trying to see if there's an angle where it doesn't look so completely distorted. And there isn't. The lighting in my bathroom is terrible, it's this harsh overhead fluorescent thing, and it just casts these shadows that make the lopsidedness look even more pronounced. Sometimes I'll even bring my phone into the bathroom and use the front-facing camera, just to see if the lens captures it differently than the mirror does, but it's always there. It's always the same swollen, crooked mess. I just... I don't understand how people can look at me and not be completely repulsed by it. It's just my face, but it feels like it's ruining my entire life.
Have you ever seen a doctor or a plastic surgeon about the swelling on your face?

No, I haven't. I mean, I've thought about it. Believe me, I've thought about it constantly. I've actually spent whole weekends just sitting at my laptop, searching for facial reconstructive surgeons in the area, looking at before-and-after galleries for hours, reading reviews, trying to figure out if there's some kind of procedure that could fix the symmetry or drain whatever is causing the swelling. I've even gone as far as filling out the little online consultation forms, typing out my name and email, and then... I just freeze. I sit there staring at the "submit" button and I can't click it. 

Because, well, part of me is terrified they'll say there's nothing they can do, that it's just how my face is built and I'm stuck with this lopsidedness forever. And then another part of me is scared that they *will* want to do surgery, and what if it goes wrong? What if they try to fix the swelling and end up making it worse, or paralyzing a nerve, and then I look even more distorted? I read this one article about a guy who had a minor procedure to correct a slight asymmetry, and he ended up with this permanent droop on one side of his mouth, and that just... it haunts me. 

Plus, how do I even explain it to them? I feel like I'd walk into a plastic surgeon's office and they'd look at me, and maybe they'd see exactly what I see and judge me for letting it get this bad before coming in. Or maybe they wouldn't know how to fix it because it's so uniquely messed up. So, no, I haven't actually gone to see anyone about it. I just sit at home, doing research, looking in the mirror, and trying to find a way to live with it, even though it feels impossible. I just don't know if a surgeon is the answer, but at the same time, I can't keep living like this, you know?
When you look in the mirror, do you think other people see your face the way you see it?

I mean, yes. Absolutely. How could they not? It's... it's not like it's some tiny, microscopic thing that you need a magnifying glass to see. It's my entire face. I mean, the swelling, the lopsidedness, it’s just glaringly obvious. When I look in the mirror, I’m not imagining things, you know? I’m looking at reality. And if I can see it that clearly, then of course everyone else can too. 

It’s actually the main thing I think about when I’m talking to people. Like yesterday, I was in the grocery store, just trying to buy some apples, and the cashier was looking at me. And I know, logically, a cashier has to look at you to ring you up and hand you your receipt, but the way she looked at me... her eyes kept darting to the swollen side of my face. I could feel it. It’s like this heavy, pulling sensation, knowing someone’s gaze is just stuck on the worst part of you. I ended up just grabbing my bags and practically running out of the store without even saying thank you, because I just couldn't stand the thought of her staring at it for one more second. 

And it’s the same with my students. I’ll be up there at the whiteboard, trying to explain the causes of the Civil War, and I’ll look out at the class, and I can just see it in their faces. Teenagers are brutal, you know? They don't have a filter. They might not say anything out loud—well, not to my face, anyway—but I can see them whispering to each other, nudging each other. And I just know, I *know*, they’re talking about how crooked my face is. I mean, if you saw someone walking around with half their face looking completely swollen and distorted, wouldn't you notice? Wouldn't you stare? It’s human nature to look at things that are abnormal, and my face is definitely abnormal. So, yes, I’m completely convinced that everyone sees exactly what I see. They’re just too polite to say anything to me directly, but I know they’re all thinking it. It's just so humiliating, constantly walking around knowing that everyone is judging this hideous thing that I can't even hide.
Have you ever asked someone you trust, like a family member or close friend, what they think about the appearance of your face?

I mean, I brought it up to my sister once, a few years ago. We were just sitting in her kitchen, and I sort of casually tried to point out the swelling, to see if she would acknowledge it. And she just immediately brushed it off. She gave me this exasperated look and said, "You look fine, stop obsessing." But, you know, family members... they’re practically obligated to lie to you, aren't they? They don't want to hurt your feelings, or maybe they just don't want to deal with the uncomfortable reality of it. So she tells me I look fine, but I know she’s just saying that to shut the conversation down. I could tell she didn't want to look too closely. So no, I don't ask anymore. I can't trust what they say anyway. 

Because I don't need someone else to tell me what I can see with my own two eyes, especially now with how much of my job involves being on camera. That’s actually where it gets really, really bad. As a teacher, we still have to do so much digital stuff—virtual parent-teacher conferences, recording backup lessons for kids who are absent—and it is an absolute nightmare for me. Before I post a recorded lesson, or even just before I join a live conference with a parent, I go into this complete tailspin. I will sit at my desk and I just keep changing the camera angle. I’ll prop my laptop up on a stack of history textbooks, then I'll take two away, then I'll tilt the screen back, just desperately trying to find some miraculous angle where the lopsidedness isn't the only thing you see. 

And if it’s a recorded lesson? I can't even tell you how much of my life I’ve wasted on those. I’ll record a ten-minute lecture on the New Deal, and then I’ll watch it back, and I just get fixated on the screen. I end up replaying clips over and over again, pausing it when I'm speaking just to stare at how distorted my jaw looks when my mouth moves. I’ll sit there alone in my classroom, literally covering parts of my face with my hand against the monitor, just trying to block out the swollen side so I can imagine what I’d look like if I were normal. And of course, I can't post a video where I look like that, so I delete it. And I re-record the whole thing. And then I find a new shadow or a new weird angle, and I delete it again. I end up re-recording the whole thing so many times that I completely blow through my planning period. I miss my prep work, I don't get any grading done, and there have been days where I've actually ended up late starting my next live class because I was so trapped in this cycle of recording and deleting. I just panic at the thought of those kids or their parents pausing the video and just staring at my face, analyzing how deformed it is. So I try to fix it, but I never can.
Have you ever considered the possibility that your face might not look as swollen or crooked to others as it does to you?

Consider that? I mean... no. Not really. I know you're trying to give me a different perspective, but I just can't. I mean, honestly, doctor, that’s... that’s the whole reason I’m here. That's why I finally made this appointment to talk to you in the first place. Because I just can’t stop seeing it. I can’t stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face, especially on those lesson videos I was just telling you about. It’s just right there, staring back at me, and it’s so pronounced, so undeniable, that there is just no way, absolutely no way, that other people are somehow magically missing it. 

And it’s completely taking over my ability to do my job. Because once I notice it—which is constantly—my brain just locks onto it. And then, when I’m actually teaching, or when I’m in a virtual staff meeting with the principal and the other teachers, or doing those parent-teacher conferences... I just feel like the students, the parents, the staff, they must *all* be staring at it instead of listening to anything I’m saying. 

I'll be sitting there, trying to explain a student's progress in AP History, or talking to my department head about curriculum changes for the semester, and I can just feel their eyes locked onto the lopsided part of my jaw. It’s like, why would they even be processing my words? My words just don't matter because this... this swelling is so loud. It’s like a neon sign blinking on the side of my head. How could a parent focus on their kid's grade, or how could a teenager focus on the Reconstruction era, when my face looks like this? They have to be staring at it. It's too distracting. I just... I can't convince myself otherwise when the evidence is right there on the screen every time I hit record. It makes me feel like a complete joke up there, just talking into the void while everyone is secretly fixated on how deformed I look.
Do you think it's possible that you're being too critical of your own appearance?

Too critical? I... I don't really think that applies here. I mean, being critical, that sounds like someone who's just a perfectionist, you know? Like someone who gets upset over a bad haircut or a tiny little blemish that nobody else can even see. But this... this isn't me nitpicking. I'm not looking for things to be upset about. I'm just looking at what's actually there. 

I honestly wish I was just being too critical. I really, really do. Because if it was just me holding myself to some impossible standard, then maybe I could just talk myself out of it. Maybe I could just take a deep breath and tell myself it's fine. But you can't talk yourself out of a physical deformity. When I get up in the morning and I walk into the bathroom... it's not like I'm pulling out a magnifying glass to hunt for flaws. I just flip on the light and it hits me all at once. The swelling, the way my jaw pulls to the side, the whole lopsided mess of it. It’s just... it’s a fact. It’s like asking me if I’m being too critical of a flat tire. It’s just flat. It’s broken. You can't positive-think your way out of it.

And I try to ignore it, I really do. I'll stand there at the sink with my toothbrush and try to focus on my hair, or just look at my eyes, just desperately trying to see a normal person looking back at me. But my eyes just go straight to the distortion. It’s so heavy and so obvious. It demands your attention. It’s not a critique I'm making, it’s just a basic observation of reality. 

So... no. No, I don't think I'm being too critical at all. I think I'm just the only one who has to live with the reality of it every single second of the day. Everyone else, the cashiers, the students, my sister... they get to look away when they feel uncomfortable. They can just change the subject or walk out of the room. But I can't look away. I'm stuck behind this face. So when I say it's swollen and crooked, I'm not being hard on myself. I'm just... I'm just seeing what's right in front of me, plain as day.
Do you think it's possible that your perception of your face might be distorted, even if you're convinced it looks a certain way?

Distorted? I... I hear what you're saying, I really do, and I know that's probably the medical way to look at it. Like my brain is just playing tricks on me or something. But... like I was trying to explain a few minutes ago, that's the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. I’m here because I absolutely cannot stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face, especially on those lesson videos I have to make. It’s not just a passing thought where I look in the mirror and think, "Oh, I look a bit off today," and then go about my business. It is completely all-consuming. 

And the hardest part—the part that makes me feel like I'm losing my mind and why I can't just accept that it's a "distorted perception"—is how it bleeds into every single interaction I have. Once I notice it on the screen, my brain just locks in. And then I just feel like the students, their parents, the other staff members... I feel like they must all be staring at it instead of listening to anything I’m saying. 

I mean, imagine trying to teach a complex unit on the Cold War, or trying to maintain authority in a room—even a virtual room—when you are entirely convinced that every single pair of eyes is just locked onto this... this deformity on your jaw. I'll be mid-sentence, trying to explain an assignment to a kid who's struggling, and suddenly my mind just spirals. I'll think, "He's not hearing a word about his essay. He's just wondering what's wrong with my face." Or I'll be in a staff development meeting, and I'll see the principal looking at my little square on the screen, and I just know she's analyzing the swelling. How could she not be? It's so distracting. It completely derails my train of thought. If it were just my perception, if it were just in my head, I feel like I'd be able to push past it and just teach. But I can't. The thought that everyone is fixated on it is so loud that it drowns everything else out. So, no, I don't think it's just my perception. I think it's a reality that is completely ruining my ability to function.
Have you ever had a time in your life when you didn't think about the appearance of your face at all?

A time when I didn't think about it at all? I... I mean, I really don't know. I'm not sure. It's... it's so hard to even imagine that right now. I guess maybe when I was a really little kid? But honestly, I can't really recall a time where I was just... completely free of it. It feels like my brain is so overwhelmed by it now that it's almost rewritten my memories. It's like... it's like trying to remember what silence sounds like when you're standing right next to a blaring siren. You just can't do it. 

Because right now, my entire day revolves around this. From the absolute second my alarm goes off at 5:30 in the morning to get ready for school, it's the very first thought that pops into my head. It's not even a conscious choice to think about it anymore, it's just this immediate, heavy dread that washes over me before I even open my eyes. And then I'm in the shower, and I'm already anticipating the bathroom mirror. I'm already bracing myself for that first look at my jaw, trying to mentally prepare for how bad the swelling is going to look that day. 

So when you ask if there was a time I didn't think about it... I just don't have a good answer for you. I really don't know. If there ever was a time, it feels like it belonged to a completely different person. Because the person I am now, the teacher who can barely look his own students in the eye during a virtual lesson... this guy can't turn it off. It's just a constant, endless loop playing in the background of everything I do. I'll be sitting at my kitchen table on a Sunday afternoon, surrounded by a stack of essays I desperately need to grade, and instead of reading about the Industrial Revolution, I'm just sitting there, staring at the wall, completely paralyzed, obsessing over the lopsidedness of my face. It just drains all the energy out of me. So... yeah, I'm really not sure. I wish I could give you a clean answer, like a specific age or something, but I just can't access a memory like that.
Can you recall any specific moment or day in the recent past when you didn't think about the appearance of your face at all?

In the recent past? No. Honestly, no. Not a single day, not even for a minute. I... I know I'm kind of repeating myself here, but I just really need you to understand how all-consuming this is. Like I said before, the whole reason I’m here, sitting in this office, is because I just absolutely can’t stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face. It's constantly on my mind, every waking second. 

And it's especially bad on those lesson videos I have to record for my classes. It's like... the camera just magnifies the deformity, you know? It puts it right there in high definition. And once I notice it—which is the exact second the recording starts or the Zoom call connects—my brain just completely hijacks me. I can't focus on the lesson plan. I can't focus on teaching. Because the whole time, I just feel like the students, or their parents who might be walking around in the background of their houses, or the other staff members watching the uploads... I feel like they must all just be staring right at my jaw instead of listening to anything I’m actually saying. 

I mean, how could they focus on a history lecture when my face looks like this? It’s all I can think about. I’ll be trying to grade papers or even just make a cup of coffee on a Saturday morning, and my mind will just pull me right back to how I looked on camera on Wednesday. So... no. Whether it was yesterday, or last week, or a month ago... there hasn't been a single moment where I got a break from it. It’s just always, always there.
Are there any areas of your life outside of teaching where you feel your perceived facial issue significantly impacts your daily activities or interactions?

Outside of teaching? I mean, if you mean outside of the actual instructional time in the classroom, then yeah, absolutely. It’s bleeding into literally every single aspect of my life and my job. 

Take the extracurriculars, for instance. I coach the basketball team at the high school, and I’m also involved in this mentoring program for at-risk students. I used to love doing those things, I really did. But lately... I’ve just completely fallen behind on all of it. The mentoring, the basketball coaching, even just my regular lesson planning... I've fallen so far behind because I just can't focus. I’ll sit down at my desk to draw up a practice schedule or review a mentee's progress report, and instead, I just get completely paralyzed thinking about my jaw. I'll start taking pictures of my profile on my phone to check the swelling, or I'll go to the staff restroom to look in the mirror, and before I know it, an hour has passed. Two hours. So much of my work never gets finished on time anymore. It just piles up and piles up on my desk, and I just stare at it, completely unable to push past the thoughts about my face.

And the worst part—the part that is really making me panic right now—is that it's not just a secret I'm keeping anymore. People are noticing that I'm dropping the ball. The administrators have actually started documenting my missed deadlines. My principal pulled me into her office last week because of coverage problems. I was supposed to be covering the cafeteria during my prep period, but I was stuck in the bathroom again, just agonizing over how lopsided my face looked under those awful fluorescent lights, and I completely missed the shift. They had to get a substitute to cover it. So now there's a paper trail. They're documenting the missed deadlines, the coverage problems, the late lesson plans... all of it. I mean, this is my career. I've worked so hard to build a life around this school, and now I’m terrified. I’m genuinely worried I’m close to losing my position, and I still can't seem to stop. I just don't know how to function when this is taking up every ounce of my mental energy.
Are you avoiding social gatherings or events outside of work because of concerns about your face?

Social gatherings outside of work? I... I mean, no, I guess not. Not really. But I think that’s mostly just because I don’t even really have a social life outside of the school right now to even avoid in the first place. I know that sounds pathetic, but it’s the truth. 

Like I was just saying, my entire world has basically shrunk down to my classroom, the staff bathroom, and my apartment. Between the teaching, the coaching that I’m failing at, and the mentoring... work is my whole life. So it’s not like I’m getting invited to all these weekend barbecues or dinner parties and explicitly RSVPing 'no' because I’m terrified of people looking at my jaw. It’s more like... I just don't do anything else anyway. 

By the time Friday afternoon finally hits, I am just so unbelievably drained. I mean, physically and mentally exhausted from spending five straight days trying to hide the lopsidedness of my face from hundreds of teenagers and my principal, and trying to desperately catch up on the mountains of grading I neglected while I was staring in the mirror. So when the weekend comes, I don't reach out to my friends. I don't make plans. Not necessarily because I'm consciously thinking, "Oh, I can't let them see my face today," but just because I have absolutely zero mental bandwidth left for any kind of normal human interaction. My brain is just completely fried from the constant, agonizing loop of worrying about the swelling all week. 

So if you're asking if there's a specific event I avoided recently, like a wedding or a happy hour... no, I don't really have anything like that to tell you. I just go to work, I struggle through the panic, I come home, and I sit at my kitchen table obsessing. There really aren't any social gatherings on my radar at all to even avoid right now.
Are there any personal relationships in your life that you feel are being negatively affected by your concerns about your face?

Personal relationships? Um... I mean, no, not really. Because like I was just saying, I don't really have any personal relationships right now. I don't have a girlfriend, I'm not dating, I barely even talk to my family these days. And it's not like I had this huge, bustling group of friends before all this started, but now... now it's just completely barren. 

I guess you could say my relationship with my mom is... well, it's non-existent, but not because of my face, just because we've never been close. And my brother lives out in Colorado, so we only text maybe twice a year anyway. So there's no one calling me, no one checking in, no one asking to come over. 

And honestly, I'm kind of relieved about it. Because if I did have a partner, or a roommate, or a best friend who wanted to hang out all the time, I don't know how I would hide this from them. I don't know how I'd explain why I spend three hours in the bathroom every night taking photos of my jaw from different angles, or why I start crying when I see myself in a store window. It's just easier this way. It's lonely, I guess, but it's easier. I don't have to pretend to be normal for anyone else when I get home. I can just lock the door, close the blinds, and deal with... all of this... by myself. So, no, there aren't any relationships being ruined, because there aren't any relationships left to ruin. It's just me and my classroom and my apartment. That's my whole world.
Do you feel like your concerns about your face are interfering with your ability to enjoy or participate in activities you used to find pleasurable?

Activities I used to find pleasurable? I mean... I guess I'd have to say no, not really, but only because I don't really have any hobbies or activities outside of work anymore. I know I mentioned the coaching and the mentoring earlier, but those are really just extensions of my job, you know? They're part of my role at the school. 

If you mean like... I don't know, playing guitar, or going hiking, or playing video games, or whatever it is normal 32-year-old guys do on their weekends... I just don't have anything like that. I never really did, to be honest. Even before all this jaw stuff started taking over my life, I was always just a workaholic. I got my degree, I got this job, and I just threw myself into it completely. I'd spend my evenings grading papers, my weekends planning lessons or watching game tape for the basketball team. I never really carved out time to develop any real hobbies. 

So it's not like there's a dusty set of golf clubs sitting in my closet that I'm too depressed or anxious to use because of my face, or a stack of unread books on my nightstand. I just... I never really had anything else. And now, of course, any free time I do have—which isn't much, considering how far behind I am at work—is entirely consumed by checking the mirror, taking pictures, and just agonizing over how asymmetrical my jawline is. But I can't really say it's interfering with my hobbies, because the hobbies just don't exist. My whole life has always been teaching, and now it's teaching and... this. Just this constant, exhausting obsession. There isn't really anything else for it to interfere with.
Have you ever considered that others might not notice your face the way you do?

Considered that they don't notice it? I mean... I try to tell myself that sometimes, but it's just impossible to believe. It's impossible. Because... well, the whole reason I even finally made this appointment, the whole reason I'm sitting here right now, is because I literally cannot stop seeing it myself, and if I can see it that clearly, how could they not? 

It started with these lesson videos. Since the pandemic, our school policy is that we have to record certain key lectures and post them to the online portal for students who are absent, or for parents who want to review the material with their kids. So I have this camera set up in the back of the classroom, and I have to watch these videos back to make sure the audio is clear and the whiteboard is visible before I upload them. And... God, it's just glaring. It's right there. On the screen, you can just see this... this crookedness. The whole left side of my jaw just looks swollen and lopsided, like my face is melting or something. 

And once I noticed it on the video, it was like a switch flipped in my brain and now I can't un-see it. I'll be standing up there at the front of the room, trying to explain the causes of the Civil War or whatever, and I'll catch my reflection in the window of the classroom door, or I'll just feel the asymmetry in my own face, and my stomach just drops. I completely lose my train of thought. Because all I can think is, "They're staring at it." 

I look out at these thirty teenagers, and I know exactly what teenagers are like. They are ruthless. They notice every little flaw, every bad haircut, every stain on your shirt. So if I can see how deformed my jaw looks on a grainy 720p video recording from thirty feet away, I know for an absolute fact that they can see it when I'm standing right in front of them. I feel like they're not even listening to a single word I'm saying about history. They're just sitting there, staring at my swollen face, probably texting each other about it under their desks. And the parents, too... when we have parent-teacher conferences, or when they watch those videos... I just know they're looking at me and thinking, "What is wrong with Mr. Davis's face?" 

So, no, I can't really convince myself that they don't notice. Because it's so obvious to me. It's all I see. And it just completely derails my ability to do my job, because I'm so hyper-aware that I'm up on this stage, basically, putting my crooked face on display for hundreds of people every single day.
Have you ever experienced recurring, intrusive thoughts or compulsions to repeat certain behaviors in other areas of your life, unrelated to your concerns about your face?

Other areas of my life? Um... no. No, I really haven't. If you mean things like, I don't know, needing to wash my hands fifty times a day or checking the stove over and over before I leave the house... I've never had anything like that. 

I mean, I'm a pretty organized person, obviously, because you kind of have to be when you're managing a classroom of thirty high schoolers. I have my lesson plans color-coded, and I keep my desk at work very tidy, and I have a very specific system for grading quizzes, but that's just... that's just being a professional, you know? It's not a compulsion. I don't feel like something terrible is going to happen if my dry-erase markers aren't lined up perfectly on the tray. 

Actually, before this whole thing with my jaw started taking over every waking second, I'd say I was probably the most boring, predictable guy you could meet. My mind was just... normal. I'd wake up at 5:30, make my drip coffee, drive to school, teach, come home, grade papers. There were no intrusive thoughts interrupting my day, no weird rituals I had to do. I'd lock my apartment door once, and I'd walk away knowing it was locked. I wouldn't even think about it again. I never had to count my steps or, I don't know, repeat words in my head. 

So it's really just... it's literally just my face. That's the only thing. It's like my brain is completely rational and functional in every single other department—I can pay my bills, I can write a semester-long syllabus, I can do all the normal adult things without any weird urges or thoughts popping up—but when it comes to my jaw and the asymmetry, all that logic just completely evaporates. So, yeah, no other compulsions or anything. It's entirely focused on the way I look.
Have you ever experienced significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life due to your preoccupation with your face?

Significant distress? I mean... yeah. God, yeah. It’s... it’s basically ruining my life, to be completely honest with you. Especially at work. 

Like I was saying earlier, teaching is everything to me. It’s my whole identity. But lately, I just... I can’t function. I’ve completely fallen behind on, well, everything. So, no, I can't really convince myself that they don't notice. Because it's so obvious to me. It's all I see.
